name: Awngtim
confidence_why: The only statement on stress that covers Awngthim and Ntra'ngith is Hale's 1966 group-level historical remark that Northern Paman shifted primary stress from the initial to the second syllable of Proto-Paman stems; no source read gives a synchronic stress rule for these lects themselves (Hale 1966 states one only for Linngithigh, Crowley 1981 only for Anguthimri, Dixon 1980 only generalities about initial-dropping languages), so the record stays undetermined.

catalog_quote: Most conspicuous among the many developments which characterize Northern Paman reflection of Proto Paman is the reduction of Initial syllables (*CV₁) by loss of initial consonants (*C₁) and loss o[r] other reduction of immediately following vowels (*V₁). Associated with initial reduction, and at least partially responsible for it is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*CV₂) in Paman stems. In all Northern Paman languages, except Uraði and its sister dialects, *C₁ was lost invariably. Even in Uraði the prevailing tendency has been toward initial loss, although *C₁ is sometimes positively reflected in that language. Short *V₁ was lost in some languages, retained in others, and metathesized in still others. Long *V·₁ was shortened in all.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level, historical statement only: in Northern Paman, including Hale's sampled Tyanngayt, Mamngayt, Ntrwa'ngayt (Awngthim) and Ntra'ngith, primary stress (non-phonemic, 'a strictly phonetic feature') shifted from the Proto-Paman initial syllable to the second syllable, and the initial consonant was then lost in all of these lects; synchronically this puts stress on the vowel of the etymological second syllable, i.e. the first vowel preceded by a consonant (the rule Hale states explicitly only for the sister language Linngithigh, p. 179). No source opened gives an Awngthim- or Ntra'ngith-specific synchronic rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Uradhi and its sister dialects sometimes retain *C1 (p. 168); short *V1 was lost, retained or metathesized depending on the language, and Awngthim metathesizes it (pp. 172-173), which affects the surface shape but is not discussed in terms of stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Diachronic remark about Paman stems across the Northern Paman subgroup, based on Hale's 1960 field data (13 lects incl. these four); not a description of a particular lect, no examples marked for stress, no word-vs-phrase discussion. Nearest lect-specific rules: Linngithigh (Hale 1966:179, first post-consonantal vowel) and Anguthimri/Mpakwithi (Crowley 1981:155-156, initial + alternating), which differ from each other.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog tyan1235 = Hale's (1966:163, 165) 'Tyanngayt-Mamngayt-Ntrwa?ngayt (collectively termed Awngtim), Ntra?ngit': three virtually identical dialects at the Embley/Mission River mouth (Mamngayt at Urquhart Point; Tyanngayt = Roth's te-ana-nedi, Thaynakwith/Tjungundji; Ntrwa'ngayth = McConnel's Ndru'angit) plus Ntra'ngith at False Pera Head/Norman River (McConnel's Ndra'angit). ISO 639-3 split these as [gwm] Awngthim (AUSTLANG Y31/Y185, dialects Y24, Y27) and [dgt] Ndra'ngith (Y39/Y27) in 2012; Glottolog keeps one language with four lects. Dixon 1980 and Crowley 1981 treat Awngthim and Ntra'ngith as dialects of Anguthimri (angu1242), whose stress rule (Crowley 1981:155-156, initial + alternating) is a different statement and a different Glottolog language; Hale 1966:165 also groups Hey's Nggerikudi (Yuputhimri, yupu1235) with these dialects. The statement quoted is Hale's Northern Paman subgroup-level remark, which explicitly covers all four lects as sample members, not a description of any one of them.

new_statements.relation_note: Near-verbatim earlier version of the Hale 1966 (AL 8(2): 167-168) sentence already in existing_statements (same shift of primary stress from the initial to the second syllable of Paman stems), so it agrees with that statement and adds nothing synchronic. Relative to the catalog record 'undetermined' it supplies only this historical claim; it does not give a modern Awngtim stress rule, so it cannot on its own move the catalog to a synchronic placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A diachronic statement, not a synchronic stress description: in the ancestor of all Northern Paman languages (the 13 sampled lects, including Tyanngayt, Mamngayt and Ntrwa'ngayt = Awngtim, and Ntra'ngit) primary stress, described as 'a strictly phonetic feature' (i.e. non-contrastive), moved from the first to the second syllable of disyllabic Paman stems, and this shift is given as a partial cause of the loss of initial consonants and initial vowels. The paper never states where stress falls in a modern Awngtim word; the compiler can only infer that the stressed proto-second syllable is what survives as the modern word-initial syllable (e.g. *minya > nya 'animal', p. 260).
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. The only qualification in the passage concerns segments: Uradhi sometimes retains *C1 (p. 256); the stress-shift statement itself is made for Paman/Northern Paman as a whole without exceptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Hale 1964 (pp. 252-254) uses Awngtim (scanned 'Awntim/Awgtim', from /awng/ 'I') as the cover term for 'three virtually identical dialects' Tyanngayt (Roth's te-ana-nadi), Mamngayt (McConnel's Mamangiti) and Ntrwa'ngayt (McConnel's Ndra?angit), clustered at the shared mouth of the Embley and Mission Rivers, and treats Ntra'ngit (False Pera Head / Norman River) as its closest relative outside the group; he identifies the dialects with Hey's Nggerikudi and McConnel's Angutimi. The stress statement is made for Northern Paman as a whole (all 13 sampled lects), not for any one dialect; the 'Awntim' examples on pp. 260-261 do not say which of the three dialects they come from.
